newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Who said what on Bosnia election day.
newsitem.headline: Who said what on Bosnia election day.

text.p: On the day Bosnians voted to choose a future for their country, battered by 43 months of war, stark differences between the wishes and hopes of the previously warring ethnic factions stood out.

The Moslems, joined with Bosnian Croats in an uneasy federation which covers 51 percent of Bosnia, campaigned for a united country while Serbs in the Bosnian Serb Republic pushed with forthright rhetoric for a separate state.
Here is a collection of quotes from voters across the country:
Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, leader of the ruling Moslem party:
"We are voting for a Bosnia where nobody will be persecuted because of his religion, nation or political orientation."
Carl Bildt, civilian peace coordinator for Bosnia:
"Overall, all across the country it is going well, good weather, a good atmosphere, it's a very good day for Bosnia."
Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic:
"(I am voting) for further progress, for Bosnia-Herzegovina, for peace, for consistency in the further implementation of the peace agreement and for state authorities on the basis of...respect."
Acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic:
"I hope that the elections throughout the territory of the Serb Republic will proceed in a democratic atmosphere and that voting will primarily be in favour of the Serb Republic."
Kresimir Zubak, Croat president of Bosnia's federation with Moslems:
"These elections are very important for fostering a long-lasting peace and rebuilding confidence between peoples to renew life and work."
Elderly Serb refugee talking to a friend outside a polling station in Serb-controlled eastern Bosnia:
"I agree. All (Moslems) should be exterminated for good. We didn't fight this bloody war so Moslems could vote in Bosnia."
Bosko Babic, local resident in Serb-held Bijeljina who found he was not registered to vote:
"I found my father who died 18 years ago on the list but not myself. He was on the list but somehow I've vanished."
Hamdija Jagic, 65, a Moslem refugee voting in former home now in Serb-controlled territory:
"This time we came here to vote. Next time we will reach our homes and the third time we will live in our homes."
Mira Zebic, a Moslem entering Serb territory to vote in her former home:
"I have no fear. I see all my husbands' former colleagues here, they all know me, I'm not scared. This is the day that I will celebrate like this was my birthday.
"We have to search for peace among people in our souls and in our children."
